w: Opened in 1911 by Mizuno Ryozo, who had helped broker Japanese emigration to Brazil and was repaid with free beans, this Ginza kissaten popularized Brazilian coffee in Japan. Taisho-era writers Akutagawa and Yoshii Isamu drank here; dark wood booths and the original blend still define Tokyo's oldest surviving cafe.
why: Widely credited as Tokyo's oldest continuously operating kissaten and the shop that introduced Brazilian coffee to Japan.

w: Housed in a wooden building dating to 1916, this Yanaka kissaten has poured coffee for local shopkeepers and students for over a century. A 2009 renovation kept the worn counter and upstairs tatami room intact. The house Kaya coffee, served slow and dark, remains the reason regulars still climb the narrow stairs.
why: One of the best-preserved pre-war kissaten buildings in Tokyo, still serving coffee from its original wooden shell.

w: Founded as Yangmu Tea Shop in 1983 by Liu Han-chieh, who staged tea ceremonies with cold-shaken Assam. In 1987 his product manager Lin Hsiu-hui tipped sweet tapioca pearls into iced tea on a whim, inventing bubble milk tea. The chain still serves that original pearl milk tea in its formal, incense-scented dining rooms.
s: Where a whim invented bubble tea in 1987
why: Widely credited as the birthplace of bubble/boba milk tea, now a global drink category.

w: Opened in 1904 by Zoroastrian immigrants from Iran, this Marine Lines institution is one of Mumbai's oldest surviving Irani cafes. Bentwood chairs, chequered floors and a glass-fronted bakery counter frame the ritual: milky Irani chai poured strong, with a bun-maska for dunking, under slow-turning ceiling fans.
why: One of the last survivors of a once-400-strong Zoroastrian cafe culture that shaped Mumbai's street-corner social life.

w: Founded in 1887 by Wu Xiqing in the last decades of the Qing dynasty, this Qianmen tea house built its name on jasmine tea scented in-house by a technique now listed as UNESCO intangible heritage. The Republican-era shopfront of blue brick and dark wood counters still weighs loose jasmine leaves by the jin.
why: Beijing's most respected jasmine tea house, its scenting technique inscribed on the UNESCO intangible heritage list.

w: A tea grower's shop since 1854, now in its seventh generation, occupying a converted tea factory beside a traditional garden in Uji, the historic source of Japan's finest matcha. Ceremonial-grade usucha is whisked to order; the signature Matcha Maruto Parfait layers ice cream, jelly and warabimochi over bitter cha.
why: A century-and-a-half-old tea grower in matcha's spiritual home town, credited with popularizing the modern matcha parfait.

w: Ippodo has traded tea on Teramachi Street since 1717, supplying imperial households and temple tea schools for three centuries. Behind the shop's wall of tea canisters, the Kaboku Tearoom whisks koicha and usucha to order at low counters, letting first-time drinkers taste grades of Uji matcha side by side.
why: One of Japan's oldest tea merchants, its in-store tearoom a rare place to taste graded matcha the way tea schools do.

w: In 1946, bartender Nguyen Van Giang, trained at the Metropole hotel, whipped egg yolk and sugar into robusta coffee to cover for a wartime milk shortage. His alley-side shop off Nguyen Huu Huan Street still serves that ca phe trung, a custardy foam over dark coffee, from the same family recipe nearly eighty years on.
why: The original creator of Vietnamese egg coffee, now imitated across Hanoi but still made here to the founder's recipe.

w: Tucked in the courtyard of the Gyeongin Museum of Fine Art, this hanok teahouse seats guests on cushions under a canopy of persimmon trees. Traditional teas like omija and jujube brew slowly in stoneware, served with roasted nuts or rice cakes in a surviving pocket of old Insadong.
s: Hanok tea garden inside a Seoul art museum
why: A working hanok teahouse inside a private art museum, among the last traditional tea gardens left in Insadong.

w: Open around the clock since 1797, this mirror-lined coffeehouse in the Khan el-Khalili bazaar has been run by seven generations of the Fishawy family. Nobel laureate Naguib Mahfouz drew on its gossip and shisha smoke for his Cairo Trilogy. Sweet tea is still boiled the old way, heated slowly in a basin of hot sand.
why: One of the Arab world's oldest continuously running coffeehouses, and the daily haunt of Nobel laureate Naguib Mahfouz.

w: Named for the French novelist who came to sketch Constantinople from this hilltop above Eyup cemetery, the cafe was restored in 1964 on the site of an older Ottoman coffeehouse he once frequented. A cable car now climbs the cypress-shaded hill to tables where Turkish coffee is still cooked over charcoal embers.
s: Hilltop Ottoman coffeehouse over the Horn
why: A restored Ottoman coffeehouse tied to novelist Pierre Loti, with one of Istanbul's most storied panoramas over the Golden Horn.

w: Founded in 1858 by a Frenchman remembered only as Monsieur Touan, Tortoni is Argentina's oldest cafe, its Tiffany-glass ceiling and marble tables unchanged since the Belle Epoque. Borges and tango singer Carlos Gardel kept regular tables here, now marked with brass plaques among the mirrors.
why: Argentina's oldest cafe and the historic anchor of Buenos Aires' literary and tango culture on Avenida de Mayo.

w: Trading under the arcades of Praca do Comercio since 1782, first as an ice house then a cafe, Martinho da Arcada keeps a table permanently reserved for poet Fernando Pessoa, who wrote here after closing time. Bica coffee is still served under the same vaulted arches above Lisbon's waterfront.
why: Lisbon's oldest cafe, famed as the haunt where modernist poet Fernando Pessoa wrote much of his fragmented body of work.

w: Opened in 1921 as Cafe Elite and renamed to chase Belle Epoque Parisian glamour, Majestic's Art Nouveau facade of carved marble and swirling ironwork hides velvet booths, gilt mirrors and moulded plaster ceilings. Once a haunt of Porto bohemians, it later lent its rococo interior an afterlife in Harry Potter lore.
why: One of Europe's most ornate Belle Epoque cafe interiors, a listed building central to Porto's early-20th-century cafe society.

w: Opened in 1884 across from the National Theatre, Slavia's Art Deco dining room of marble, leather booths and river-view windows drew Capek, Seifert and, in the 1920s, exiled Russian poet Marina Tsvetaeva. Later a refuge for dissidents around Vaclav Havel, it remains Prague's definitive literary coffeehouse.
why: The gathering place of Prague's writers and, later, its Velvet Revolution-era dissidents, opposite the National Theatre.

w: Founded in 1914 by Marco Lovrinovich, San Marco's Vienna Secession interior of dark wood and etched mirrors survived arson during the First World War and became the wartime refuge of James Joyce and Italo Svevo. Books still line its walls today, half cafe and half bookshop, in a city built on coffee and empires.
why: Trieste's central literary cafe, its Vienna Secession interior tied to the city's Habsburg-era coffee and writing culture.

w: Opened in 1927 by Armenian immigrant Khachik Madikians, this French-style cafeteria on what was then Naderi Street became the preferred haunt of writers Sadegh Hedayat and Jalal Al-e-Ahmad through the 1930s and 1950s. Confiscated in 1979 and later returned to the founder's family, it is now a listed monument.
why: The historic hub of mid-century Iranian literary life, now a protected national monument still run by the founder's family.

w: Down a narrow alley off Lebuh Campbell, this Hainanese kopitiam has toasted bread over charcoal since 1950, run now by a third generation of the founding family. Soft-boiled kampung eggs, kaya toast and coffee filtered through a cloth sock draw queues that spill past the open charcoal stove into the lane outside.
why: One of George Town's most-queued Hainanese kopitiam, still hand-toasting bread over open charcoal after three generations.

w: Set beside the lake in Renmin Park and dating to around 1923, Heming is Chengdu's best-known open-air teahouse, its bamboo armchairs packed shoulder to shoulder under plane trees. Waiters still pour long-spouted copper kettles tableside; between refills of jasmine tea, ear-cleaners and fortune tellers work the crowd.
why: The emblematic teahouse of Chengdu's unhurried tea culture, still filled daily with mahjong tiles and long-spout kettle pours.

w: Opened in 1888 on the Paseo de Recoletos, Gijon became the home of Spain's tertulia tradition, the informal round-table debates that drew Lorca, Bunuel and Dali before the civil war. Hemingway and Truman Capote later took tables here too. A literary prize still bears its name, awarded from beneath its mirrored walls.
why: The definitive Madrid tertulia cafe, cradle of the Generation of '27 and namesake of a major Spanish literary prize.

w: Coffee has been poured in this Kleine Fleischergasse building since 1711, one of Europe's oldest surviving coffee houses. A baroque relief of an Arab handing coffee to a cherub marks the door. Bach's Collegium Musicum played here, and Schumann's circle of Romantic composers later claimed the regulars' table.
why: One of Europe's oldest working coffee houses, a regular haunt of Bach, Goethe and Schumann across three centuries.

w: Opened in 1912 inside a former 17th-century mansion and dairy on Tacuba Street, this cafe-restaurant survived the Mexican Revolution and a 1936 political assassination on its premises. Talavera tiles, a hand-painted mural and hot chocolate whisked with a wooden molinillo remain unchanged from its early years.
why: A century-old Mexico City institution whose chocolate and mural-lined dining room inspired the rock band that took its name.

w: Housed since 1942 inside the former Albert Hall on College Street, this worker-cooperative coffee house hosted Subhas Chandra Bose and the Hungry Generation poets under ceiling fans and peeling murals. Uniformed bearers still carry filter coffee between tables of students debating politics for hours.
s: Bengal's addas over filter coffee since 1942
why: The intellectual heart of College Street, an unbroken hub of Kolkata's coffeehouse debate culture since 1942.

w: Trading from the same Killiney Road corner shophouse since 1919, this Hainanese coffee shop is reckoned Singapore's oldest, its marble-top tables and rattan chairs a holdover from colonial-era kopitiam design. Kaya toast is still charcoal-grilled and dunked in soft-boiled eggs seasoned with pepper and soy.
why: Singapore's longest-running Hainanese coffee shop, a template later franchised worldwide but still centred on its original shophouse.

w: Founded by a family who fled wartime China for Vietnam before settling on Grant Avenue, Red Blossom has sourced tea directly from farmers in China and Taiwan since the 1980s. Its narrow Chinatown showroom stocks over a hundred single-origin teas, from aged pu-erh to hand-fired oolong, weighed loose at the counter.
why: San Francisco Chinatown's most respected tea merchant, sourcing directly from small farms across China and Taiwan since the 1980s.

w: Trading since 1839 on Aiolou Street overlooking the Athens Central Market, Oraia Ellas is among the city's oldest kafeneia, its marble tables set beneath a view of the Acropolis. Hans Christian Andersen is said to have stopped by soon after it opened; Greek coffee is still boiled slow in sand.
why: One of Athens' oldest surviving kafeneia, a working link to the city's 1830s coffeehouse culture with the Acropolis in view.

w: Bought from its Italian founders in 1953 and renamed for the words Torrefazione Moderna Caffe, Tomoca was the first company to roast Ethiopian coffee commercially outside the home. Regulars still drink standing at the Piassa counter, ordering the macchiato style the shop is credited with popularizing.
why: Ethiopia's most storied coffee roaster, credited with commercializing the Italian-influenced macchiato culture of Addis Ababa.

w: Started as a Gage Street cart in 1952 by Chaozhou immigrant Lam Muk-ho, Lan Fong Yuen is credited with inventing silk-stocking milk tea, filtering black tea through cloth strainers stained dark enough to resemble stockings. The stall grew into a cha chaan teng, still pulling tea in steaming arcs.
why: The originator of Hong Kong's silk-stocking milk tea, a technique that became the template for cha chaan teng tea culture citywide.
